data.title: MDQ Specification Audit: True/False
data.scope: The true-false question type: `docs/question-types/true-false.md`, `schema/true-false.yaml`, the shared choice list rules in `docs/references/choices.md`, and the parts of `docs/references/grammar.md`, `docs/question-types/question-base.md`, `docs/exam.md`, `docs/responses.md` and the corpus that concern true-false.

data.title: Contradictions
Ambiguities
Omissions
Inconsistencies
Grammar violations
Schema mismatches
True/false all-or-nothing gives partial credit
data.snippet:
* **all-or-nothing**: The student must mark all choices with the correct marking
  or abstain. Any mistake in the marked choices gives zero points. If all marked
  choices are correct, the student gets a score proportional to the number of
  correct markings (`correctly marked / total number of choices`).
data.description: Under true/false `all-or-nothing`, a response with no mistakes scores `correctly marked / total`, so `[T, F, _, _]` scores 0.5 (table at line 223, and `examples/grading/true-false.yaml:45-46`). GLOSSARY.md defines All-or-nothing as 'scoring 1 only when every part is correct, and 0 otherwise', and multiple selection (`docs/question-types/multiple-selection.md:114-115`) and fill-in (`docs/question-types/fill-in.md:327`) follow the glossary. The true/false rule is 'partial, unless there is a mistake'.
data.impact: An exam that sets `grading: all-or-nothing` for every type gets two different meanings. An instructor who expects no credit for an incomplete true/false answer gives 0.5 to a student who judged half of the statements.
data.fix: Either make true/false all-or-nothing score 1 only when every statement is judged correctly (an abstention counts as a mistake), or keep the current rule, give it a different name, and update the glossary. The first option agrees with the glossary and the other types.

data.title: Locale text refers to an `id` row that the table does not have
data.snippet:
dedicated warning, `false-friend-true-false-marker`. The `id` row has no
mismatched form, so `locale-mismatched-true-false-marker` is never issued for
it.
data.description: The locale table at lines 160-164 has rows only for `en`, `pt` and `es`. There is no `id` row. Line 155-157 says a language not in the table has no expectation, so `id` already gets no `locale-mismatched-true-false-marker`; the sentence about an `id` row with 'no mismatched form' describes a row that does not exist.
data.impact: A reader cannot tell whether `id` is meant to be in the table (with which letters) or not.
data.fix: Delete the sentence about the `id` row, or add an `id` row (`B` / `S`? `T` / `F`?) and define what 'no mismatched form' means.

data.title: The spec does not define which markers are locale-mismatched
data.snippet:
Implementations MAY issue warnings for True/False letters that are incompatible
with the locale for the question. For instance, if `locale: pt-BR`, it may
expect `V` and `F` -- for "verdadeiro" (true) and "falso" (false) -- and could
issue a warning if `T` is used instead.
data.description: 'Incompatible with the locale' is defined only by one example (`T` under `pt`). Open cases: is `S`, `对` or `错` under `pt` mismatched? Is a WARNING letter such as `W` under `pt` also mismatched, or only `unlisted-true-false-marker`? Is lowercase `t` mismatched (case-insensitive)? mdq-py warns for every TRUE or FALSE letter outside the expected pair, case-insensitively, and never for a WARNING letter: under `pt-BR` it flags `S`, `t`, `对`, `错` and not `W`.
data.impact: Two implementations can report different warnings for the same document.
data.fix: State the rule: under a locale in the table, a marker in the TRUE or FALSE category whose case-folded form is not the expected letter of its category is mismatched. WARNING letters get only `unlisted-true-false-marker`.
data.conditions: `locale` with a language subtag in the table.

data.title: Locale warning is a MAY in the prose and a warning in the table
data.snippet: Implementations MAY issue warnings for True/False letters that are incompatible
data.description: The audit convention maps MAY to info, SHOULD to warning. The prose says implementations MAY issue `locale-mismatched-true-false-marker`, but the Additional Rules row (line 247) and `docs/lint-codes.md:28` give it the warning level. The same section uses SHOULD for `false-friend-true-false-marker` (line 172).
data.impact: The requirement level of the rule is unclear.
data.fix: Change the prose to SHOULD (keep warning), or move the rule to info. SHOULD agrees with the corpus (`examples/valid/true-false/locale-mismatch.lint.json`).

data.title: NFC rule mixes combining sequences with non-NFC single code points
data.snippet:
* "One code point", not one grapheme cluster. A base letter followed by a
  combining mark is two code points and is not a valid marker. Implementations
  MAY report, at the info level, a marker that is not in NFC form: in NFC,
  precomposed forms are single code points.
data.description: The bullet says a combining sequence is invalid (an error), then in the same breath offers an info for a marker 'not in NFC form', with the reason 'in NFC, precomposed forms are single code points'. That reason is about combining sequences, which are already `malformed-true-false-marker`. The info can only apply to a single code point whose NFC form differs, such as U+212B ANGSTROM SIGN (NFC U+00C5) or U+212A KELVIN SIGN (NFC `K`), which is the case `examples/valid/true-false/non-nfc-marker.yaml` tests and `docs/lint-codes.md:39` describes. The table row 'is not a single code point in NFC form' can be read as covering combining sequences too.
data.impact: An implementer can emit the info for combining sequences, or miss the singleton case.
data.fix: Split the bullet: a combining sequence is two code points and is `malformed-true-false-marker`; a single code point that NFC changes (U+212B to U+00C5) MAY get `non-nfc-true-false-marker`. Reword the table row to 'is a single code point that NFC changes'.

data.title: Case-insensitivity and compatibility forms of letters are not defined
data.snippet:
We only show the upper case versions of each symbol. Each set must be expanded
with lowercase versions as well; the CJK characters have no case and are used
as-is.
data.description: The spec does not say which case mapping applies. mdq-py uses case folding: `[ſ]` (U+017F LATIN SMALL LETTER LONG S) folds to `s` and reads as TRUE with no warning. The fullwidth letters that CJK input methods produce are WARNING letters: `[Ｆ]` (U+FF26) reads as true with only `unlisted-true-false-marker`, so a statement the author marked false is graded as true. A titlecase letter (`Lt`, such as U+01C5) is a WARNING letter too.
data.impact: Implementations that use lowercase mapping, case folding or NFKC give different categories for the same marker. The fullwidth `Ｆ` case flips the answer key with only a warning.
data.fix: Define the comparison: for example, NFKC then case folding before the category lookup, so `Ｆ` is FALSE and `ſ` is TRUE. Or keep exact comparison of the letter and its simple lowercase, and make a fullwidth `Ｔ`/`Ｆ` an error. Add corpus examples for the chosen rule.

data.title: Responses do not say that a `null` statement value is an abstention
data.snippet:
A mapping from statement id to the judgement the student made. Unlike multiple
selection, an absent key is **not** a false: it is an abstention, and the
student may deliberately leave a statement unjudged.
data.description: The response is 'a mapping of statement id to boolean' (line 29), and only an absent key is an abstention. `examples/grading/true-false.yaml:15-16` and its 'Explicit null' cases (line 68) treat `earth-is-flat: null` as an abstention too. The spec does not say whether `null` is an abstention or a malformed response, nor what a non-boolean value (`"T"`, `1`) is.
data.impact: An implementation that follows the spec text rejects a response that the shared grading corpus requires it to accept.
data.fix: In docs/responses.md, say that a `null` value is the same as an absent key, and that any other non-boolean value is a malformed response. Do the same for multiple selection if `null` is allowed there.

data.title: `uniform-true-false-answers` is not described in the prose
data.snippet: | choices[].correct  | info     | uniform-true-false-answers               | the statements are all true or all false                   |
data.description: The Additional Rules table and `docs/lint-codes.md:51` list the info, but no section of true-false.md mentions it or gives it a MAY.
data.impact: The rule exists only in the tables, without its rationale.
data.fix: Add a sentence, for example under Grading: 'Implementations MAY report, at the info level, a question whose statements are all true or all false (`uniform-true-false-answers`).'

data.title: Abstention is called skip, unmarked, missing and unjudged
data.snippet: Including abstentions is deliberate: a student who skips a statement because
data.description: GLOSSARY.md defines Abstention and says to avoid 'skip' for it; Skip is the absence of a response to a whole question. Line 183 says 'skips a statement'. The Grading section uses 'missing marking' (201), 'abstain' (205), 'unmarked' (210-211), and the table uses `_` without saying what it is.
data.impact: 'skips a statement' collides with the defined term Skip, which has different grading (no feedback).
data.fix: Use 'abstains on a statement' / 'abstention' throughout, and say in the table intro that `_` is an abstention.

data.title: False-friend footnote speaks of an `S` 'meaning false'
data.snippet:
[^4]: An `S` marker meaning false under `locale: id` SHOULD get
`false-friend-true-false-marker`, see [locale](#locale).
data.description: An `S` never means false: it is always TRUE (line 83). The intent of the author cannot be known, and the rule (line 248) fires for every `S` under `id`. The footnote is also attached to the `locale-mismatched` row, where it does not apply.
data.impact: A reader may think the lint needs to guess intent.
data.fix: 'Every `S` marker under `locale: id` SHOULD get `false-friend-true-false-marker`.' Attach the footnote only to that row.

data.title: TRUE letters written as one code span `TVS`
data.snippet: * **TRUE**: `TVS`, plus 对 (Mandarin "dui") and 真 (Japanese "shin")
data.description: `TVS` reads as a three-letter string. The CJK letters on the same line are not in code spans.
data.impact: Minor: a reader may take `TVS` as one marker.
data.fix: `T`, `V`, `S`, `对` and `真`; the same for the FALSE line.

data.title: Type inference 'a value is a letter' does not say spaces are removed
data.snippet: 3. a value is a letter: true/false;
data.description: The true/false `value` rule allows `ws` around the letter (`[ T ]`), and `examples/valid/true-false/spaced-markers.mdq.md` infers true/false from such markers. Rule 3 says 'a value is a letter', and the value of `[ T ]` is ` T `. 'letter' also does not link to its definition in true-false.md (one code point in `\p{L}`).
data.impact: A literal reading infers multiple selection for `[ T ]` lists, then reports every item as `foreign-choice-marker`.
data.fix: 'a value, without the `ws` around it, is a [letter](true-false.md#body)'. Same for rules 1 and 2 (`[ x ]`, `[ * ]`).

data.title: Cyrillic and Greek look-alikes of `T`, `F` and `X` are WARNING letters
data.snippet: * **WARNING**: Every other letter, except `X` and `x`.
data.description: Cyrillic `Т` (U+0422), `Х` (U+0425) and Greek `Τ` (U+03A4), `Χ` (U+03A7) look like `T` and `X`. A list of only Cyrillic `[Х]` items is inferred as true/false and every statement reads as true, with `unlisted-true-false-marker`. Russian 'верно' starts with Cyrillic `В`, which looks like Latin `B`. The warning catches these, but its message cannot tell the author why.
data.impact: Low: the warning fires, but the cause is invisible in most fonts.
data.fix: Optionally mention look-alike letters in the WARNING paragraph, so implementations can give a better message.

data.text: The `marker`/`correct` split is well argued: `correct` drives grading, `marker` keeps round-tripping and enables the WARNING and locale lints, and the spec says which lints are lost without `marker`.
The symmetric and partial rows of the grading table agree with the prose and with examples/grading/true-false.yaml, including abstentions and explicit-null cases.
The corpus covers every true/false lint code in the Additional Rules table, including CJK, non-BMP, non-NFC, false-friend lowercase and locale without expectation (examples/valid/true-false/).
Feedback rules for true/false (wrong and abstained statements, document order, none on skip) agree with GLOSSARY.md Feedback and docs/responses.md Skipping.

data.title: Type inference compares the raw value, with its ws, to `x`, `*` and a letter
data.description: choices.md defines the value as "the text in the marker", and the true-false rule `value : ws? (true | false) ws?` accepts spaces and tabs around the letter. The inference rules test whether the value "is" `x`, `*` or a letter, and do not say to remove the `ws` first. Counter-example: `* [ T ] a` / `* [ F] b`. The values are ` T ` and ` F`, which are not letters, so rule 4 makes the list multiple selection, and every item is then a `foreign-choice-marker`. The valid corpus file `examples/valid/true-false/spaced-markers.mdq.md` expects true/false. The same applies to `[ x ]` and `[ * ]` (`examples/valid/multiple-selection/uppercase-x.mdq.md`, `examples/valid/multiple-choice/spaced-values.mdq.md`).
data.impact: A literal reading turns valid spaced markers into errors; the prose and the corpus disagree.
data.fix: State that the inference rules apply to the value without the `ws` at its start and end (the part inside the optional `ws?` of each `value` rule).

data.title: The `true` and `false` rules are never defined, and WARNING letters have no rule
data.snippet: value : ws? (true | false) ws?
data.description: No snippet defines `true` or `false`; `scripts/spec_audit.py` compiles the snippet only with stubs. The letter sets exist only in prose (lines 83-98), and the WARNING category, which means true, is not visible in the rule. A reader cannot tell from the grammar that `[Q]` matches `true`. Testing needed a hand-built grammar: `true : /[TtVvSs对真]/`, `false : /[Ff错偽]/`, and a third alternative for every other letter except `X`/`x`.
data.impact: The grammar does not decide which markers are valid; implementations rebuild the sets from prose.
data.fix: Define the rules in the snippet, for example `true : TRUE_LETTER | WARNING_LETTER`, `false : FALSE_LETTER`, with terminals for each set, and explain `WARNING_LETTER` as a letter outside the other sets and outside `X`/`x`.

data.title: `\p{L}` breaks the regex dialect rule of the common grammar
data.snippet:
A **letter** is exactly one Unicode code point whose General_Category is one of
`Lu`, `Ll`, `Lt`, `Lm` or `Lo` -- that is, the character class written `\p{L}`
in regex engines that support Unicode properties.
data.description: grammar.md ("Regex dialect") says terminals use only explicit character classes that match the same characters in Python `re`, JavaScript `RegExp` and JSON Schema `pattern`. `\p{L}` does not meet this: `re.compile(r'\p{L}')` raises `bad escape \p` in Python 3.13; in JavaScript without the `u` flag, `/^\p{L}$/` is a literal `p{L}` and does not match `p` or `真`; without `u`, `/^[^\]]$/` does not match U+20000 (two UTF-16 units). Lark's default `re` backend cannot use it either; the explicit class built from `unicodedata` for the test is about 10 KB.
data.impact: The letter terminal cannot be written in the dialect the spec mandates, so each implementation picks its own engine and flags.
data.fix: State the exception in grammar.md: the letter test uses the Unicode General_Category of one code point (Python `unicodedata.category`, JavaScript `/^\p{L}$/u`), not a regex of the common dialect.

data.title: The Unicode version of the letter test is not fixed, so Python and JavaScript disagree
data.snippet:
A **letter** is exactly one Unicode code point whose General_Category is one of
`Lu`, `Ll`, `Lt`, `Lm` or `Lo`
data.description: General_Category changes between Unicode versions. Python 3.13 here has Unicode 15.1; Node has Unicode 17.0. U+10D50 GARAY CAPITAL LETTER A (Unicode 16.0) is `Cn` in Python and matches `/^\p{L}$/u` in Node. Counter-example: `* [\u{10D50}] a` / `* [F] b` is a valid true/false list in mdq-js and, in mdq-py, rule 4 of type inference does not apply because rule 3 does (`F`), but the first value is a `foreign-choice-marker`. A list of only such letters is true/false in one implementation and multiple selection in the other.
data.impact: The same document gets a different type or different errors in each implementation, which grammar.md explicitly tries to prevent.
data.fix: Fix a minimum Unicode version for the letter test, or state that letters unassigned in that version are not letters.

data.title: Fullwidth and mathematical forms of `F` are WARNING letters and mean true
data.snippet:
* **FALSE**: `F`, plus 错 (Mandarin "cuo") and 偽 (Japanese "gi")
* **WARNING**: Every other letter, except `X` and `x`.
data.description: `Ｆ` (U+FF26 FULLWIDTH LATIN CAPITAL LETTER F, `Lu`) is not in FALSE, so it is a WARNING letter and means true. A CJK input method produces it easily, and the spec targets CJK authors (对, 真, 错, 偽). The same holds for `ℱ` (U+2131) and `𝐅` (U+1D405); all three NFKC-normalize to `F`. Counter-example: `* [Ｆ] O Sol gira em torno da Terra.` is graded true, with only an `unlisted-true-false-marker` warning. The grammar test accepts it as a WARNING letter.
data.impact: An author who meant false gets an inverted answer key, with a warning instead of an error.
data.fix: Classify a letter by its NFKC form (or by its fullwidth form) before the TRUE/FALSE lookup, or make letters whose NFKC form is in FALSE or `X`/`x` an error.

data.title: Look-alikes of `X` make a list true/false instead of multiple selection
data.snippet:
2. a value is `x` or `X`: multiple selection;
3. a value is a letter: true/false;
data.description: Only ASCII `x`/`X` select multiple selection. Cyrillic `Х` (U+0425), Greek `Χ` (U+03A7), fullwidth `Ｘ` (U+FF38) and `ˣ` (U+02E3, `Lm`) are letters, so rule 3 applies. Counter-example: `* [Х] Manaus` / `* [ ] Santos` is inferred true/false, and `[ ]` is a `foreign-choice-marker`; the message points at the wrong item. A list of only `[Х]` is a true/false list with every statement true.
data.impact: Confusing errors, or a wrong question type, for a marker that looks correct.
data.fix: Treat letters whose NFKC form or confusable skeleton is `x`/`X` as rule 2, or report them with a dedicated lint.

data.title: `\p{L}` includes signs that do not look like letters
data.snippet:
A **letter** is exactly one Unicode code point whose General_Category is one of
`Lu`, `Ll`, `Lt`, `Lm` or `Lo`
data.description: `Lm` and `Lo` contain characters that read as punctuation or symbols: `ˆ` (U+02C6), `ー` (U+30FC KATAKANA-HIRAGANA PROLONGED SOUND MARK, looks like a dash), `々` (U+3005), and the ordinal indicators `ª` (U+00AA) and `º` (U+00BA), common in pt-BR. Counter-example: `* [ー] a` is accepted as a WARNING letter and means true, while the spec excludes `✓`, `×` and `〇` because they are not letters.
data.impact: The goal of the exclusion ("marks that look like answers but are not letters are NOT valid") is only partly met.
data.fix: Restrict the WARNING set to `Lu`, `Ll`, `Lt` and `Lo` minus a short exclusion list, or accept the behaviour and list these examples.

data.title: Case-insensitivity does not say lowercase mapping or case folding
data.snippet:
We only show the upper case versions of each symbol. Each set must be expanded
with lowercase versions as well;
data.description: Line 47 says the letters are case-insensitive; line 96 says the sets are expanded with lowercase versions. These differ for `ſ` (U+017F LATIN SMALL LETTER LONG S): `'ſ'.casefold()` is `s`, but `ſ` is not the lowercase of `S`. With case folding, `[ſ]` is TRUE with no warning; with lowercase expansion, it is WARNING and gets `unlisted-true-false-marker`. The meaning is true in both, so only the lint differs.
data.impact: Implementations can disagree on the `unlisted-true-false-marker` warning.
data.fix: List the exact sets (`T t V v S s 对 真`, `F f 错 偽`) and say no other mapping applies.

data.title: The NFC prose implies the info lint covers combining sequences, which are errors
data.snippet: | choices[].marker   | info     | non-nfc-true-false-marker                | is not a single code point in NFC form[^2]                 |
data.description: Lines 65-68 say a base letter plus a combining mark is not a valid marker, then that implementations MAY report a marker not in NFC form, because NFC forms are single code points. This reads as if the info lint is for `[e\u0301]`, but that input fails the grammar (rejected in the test) and is a `foreign-choice-marker` error. The table row "is not a single code point in NFC form" can be read as "is not (one code point in NFC)", which also covers the two-code-point case. The lint actually targets one code point that NFC changes, such as `Å` (U+212B, `examples/valid/true-false/non-nfc-marker.yaml`) or U+2F946 (NFC `真`); `docs/lint-codes.md:39` says so.
data.impact: Readers can expect an info lint where the spec gives an error.
data.fix: Reword as in lint-codes.md: "is one code point, but not its own NFC form", and give `Å` U+212B as the example.

data.title: Some valid single-code-point markers are not one code point after NFC
data.snippet:
* "One code point", not one grapheme cluster. A base letter followed by a
  combining mark is two code points and is not a valid marker.
data.description: `क़` U+0958 DEVANAGARI LETTER QA is one `Lo` code point, so `* [क़] a` is a valid WARNING marker (accepted in the test). Its NFC form is two code points (U+0915 U+093C, a composition exclusion). An editor or pipeline that normalizes to NFC turns the valid marker into a `foreign-choice-marker`. Conversely, `[é]` is valid as U+00E9 and invalid as `e` + U+0301. The spec does not say whether the parser normalizes the source.
data.impact: Validity of a marker can change when an editor normalizes the file.
data.fix: State that the parser does not normalize the source, and mention composition exclusions next to the NFC lint.

data.title: Two error codes apply to `[x]` and `[TF]` in a list forced to true/false
data.snippet:
| choices[]          | error    | foreign-choice-marker                    | must use a value allowed in a true/false list              |
| choices[].marker   | error    | malformed-true-false-marker              | must be a single letter[^2]                                |
| choices[].marker   | error    | reserved-true-false-marker               | must not be `X` or `x`[^2]                                 |
data.description: With `type: true-false`, `* [x] a` fails the `value` rule (`foreign-choice-marker`) and also has a marker `x` (`reserved-true-false-marker`); `* [TF] a` and `* [✓] a` match both `foreign-choice-marker` and `malformed-true-false-marker`. The table does not say which one a markdown document gets. The corpus uses `foreign-choice-marker` for markdown (`examples/invalid/true-false-symbol-marker`) and the other two only for YAML (`examples/invalid/model-only/`), and `docs/lint-codes.md:84` ties them to the `marker` field, but true-false.md does not state this.
data.impact: Implementations can report different codes for the same markdown input.
data.fix: Say in the table that `malformed-true-false-marker` and `reserved-true-false-marker` apply to the `marker` field of model input, and that a markdown value outside the `value` rule is `foreign-choice-marker`.

data.title: An item with other block content fails the `item` rule, and no error code is given
data.snippet: item      : ws? "[" value VALUE_END ws? (CHOICE_ID ws?)? md_inline* nl lazy_line* (blank_line* observations)?
data.description: The rule allows one paragraph of text and then the observations. CommonMark gives an item more blocks, and these inputs fail the rule in the test: a second paragraph (`* [F] Flat` / blank / `  More text.`), a nested list (`* [T] a` / `  * sub`), a fenced code block, and text after the feedback (`  > fb` / blank / `  Later text.`). The spec states `parse-error` for a second feedback block, but not for these. It does not say if the list stops being a choice list, if the item is a `parse-error`, or if the extra blocks join the text.
data.impact: Implementations can treat a common authoring mistake differently.
data.fix: State the result: for example, any block in a choice item other than the first paragraph, the feedback and the comment is a `parse-error`.

data.text: The true-false `value` rule, with `true : /[TtVvSs对真]/`, `false : /[Ff错偽]/` and the WARNING class built from General_Category, accepts `[T]`, `[t]`, `[V]`, `[S]`, `[F]`, `[f]`, `[对]`, `[真]`, `[错]`, `[偽]`, `[ T ]`, `[\tT\t]`, `[é]` (U+00E9) and the astral letter U+20000, and rejects `[X]`, `[x]`, `[TF]`, `[ ]`, `[]`, `[✓]`, `[×]`, `[〇]`, `[1]`, `[*]` and `[e\u0301]`, as the prose states (Lark Earley test).
`ws` is only space and tab, so `[\u00a0T]` and `[\u3000F]` fail the `value` rule, which agrees with the rule that a Unicode space where the grammar expects `ws` is text.
`VALUE_END` refuses a bracket followed by `(` or `[`: `* [T](http://x) a` and `* [T][a] a` fail the `item` rule and stay links, in line with `CHOICE_MARK` and `CHOICE_ID`.

The `item` grammar is ambiguous about the `ws` after the value and about whether `[brasilia]` is a `CHOICE_ID` or text (2 and 4 parse trees in the Earley test), but the prose settles both: the bracket that matches `CHOICE_ID` is always the id, and the text excludes the `ws` after the value and the id. `* [T] [brasilia]` gives an empty text and `* [T] [V] text` gives the id `V`.

Feedback and comment rules hold for true-false items in the test: `> fb` then `! c` is accepted, a lazy line continues the feedback, a blank line before the feedback is accepted, an empty `>` line is part of the block, `![x](y.png)` is a lazy line and not a comment, `2. two` is a lazy line and `1. one` is not, and a second `>` block after a comment fails the rule (the stated `parse-error`).

Type inference decides mixed lists: `[x]` with `[T]` is multiple selection by rule 2 and `[T]` is a `foreign-choice-marker`; `[ ]` with `[F]` is true/false by rule 3 and `[ ]` is a `foreign-choice-marker` (as `examples/invalid/true-false-blank-marker` expects); `[✓]`/`[✗]` falls to rule 4. The X/x exclusion of the WARNING set matches rule 2, so no letter is claimed by both types.

No compatibility ideograph whose NFC form is a TRUE or FALSE letter changes the meaning: the only ones found, U+2F946 and U+2F947 (NFC 真), are WARNING letters and so also mean true (scan of all `\p{L}` code points with `unicodedata`, Unicode 15.1).

data.title: The `marker`/`correct` agreement rule and the reserved `X` rule exist only in the table
data.snippet:
| choices[].marker   | error    | reserved-true-false-marker               | must not be `X` or `x`[^2]                                 |
| choices[].marker   | error    | true-false-marker-disagrees-with-correct | must agree with `correct` according to its category[^3]    |
data.description: The Choices section says a statement records the letter in two fields, but never states that they MUST agree (a FALSE letter with `correct: true`, or a TRUE or WARNING letter with `correct: false`). The prose also never says that a `marker` of `X` or `x` is an error: line 49 and line 85 only exclude `X` from the letters that have a truth value. Both rules are errors that appear only in the Additional Rules table. The WARNING case (`N` with `correct: false` is an error, `examples/invalid/model-only/true-false-marker-disagrees-warning.yaml`) is described only in `docs/lint-codes.md:88`.
data.impact: A reader of the prose cannot know that a YAML document with `marker: F, correct: true` or `marker: X` is invalid, nor that a WARNING letter forces `correct: true`.
data.fix: Under Choices, add: 'When `marker` is present, its category MUST agree with `correct`: FALSE letters with `false`, TRUE and WARNING letters with `true` (`true-false-marker-disagrees-with-correct`). `marker` MUST NOT be `X` or `x` (`reserved-true-false-marker`).'
data.conditions: Documents written in YAML or JSON, where `marker` and `correct` are independent.

data.title: `marker` is 'exactly as it was written', but the `ws` inside the brackets is dropped
data.snippet: | marker  | string  | The letter itself, exactly as it was written.           |
data.description: The value rule allows `ws` around the letter (`[ T ]`, `[F ]`, `[\tT\t]`), and `examples/valid/true-false/spaced-markers.yaml` stores `marker: T` for each. The spec says `marker` is the letter 'exactly as it was written' and 'stored verbatim', and that it keeps the ability 'to be written back out unchanged' (line 142-143). It does not say that the spaces are removed, nor that spacing is lost on a round trip.
data.impact: An implementation that reads 'verbatim' literally stores ` T `, which then fails `malformed-true-false-marker` and the schema `maxLength: 1`.
data.fix: Say that `marker` is the letter of the value without the `ws` around it, and that only the letter and its case are kept.

data.title: The schema and `malformed-true-false-marker` both reject a marker that is not one code point
data.snippet: | choices[].marker   | error    | malformed-true-false-marker              | must be a single letter[^2]                                |
data.description: The schema has `minLength: 1` and `maxLength: 1` on `marker`, so an empty, multi-character or combining-sequence marker is a schema violation. The Additional Rules table lists the same check as `malformed-true-false-marker` without '(schema)', and `docs/question-types/question-base.md:329` says the table lists only rules the schema does not capture. `docs/lint-codes.md:84` says `malformed-true-false-marker` covers an empty or longer marker. `examples/invalid/true-false-combining-mark-marker.yaml:3` says the schema 'rejects it too', but its `.lint.json` expects only `malformed-true-false-marker`, and mdq-py reports no `schema-error` for `marker: ""` or `marker: "TRUE"`. The spec does not say which code wins when both apply.
data.impact: An implementation that reports schema errors as `schema-error` fails the corpus for these documents, or reports two errors for one defect.
data.fix: Either remove `minLength`/`maxLength` from the schema and leave the check to `malformed-true-false-marker`, or state that a dedicated code replaces `schema-error` when both apply to the same field.

data.title: Schema accepts any single code point as `marker`
data.snippet:
marker:
        type: string
data.description: The spec defines `marker` as one code point in `\p{L}`, other than `X` or `x` (true-false.md:52-64, 236-237). The schema checks only the length, so `marker: "1"`, `marker: "✓"` and `marker: X` pass it. Its description says 'The single letter', which the schema does not enforce.
data.impact: A consumer that relies on the schema alone accepts markers the spec forbids.
data.fix: Add `pattern: "^\\p{L}$"` and `not: {enum: [X, x]}`, or say in the description that the letter and reserved checks are model rules (`malformed-true-false-marker`, `reserved-true-false-marker`). The first option interacts with the code-precedence question of the length check.

data.title: Schema `marker` description omits the agreement check
data.snippet:
carries the meaning, but the letter itself is needed to warn
          about WARNING letters and locale mismatches, and to
          round-trip the document unchanged.
data.description: The description lists the uses of `marker` but omits the error `true-false-marker-disagrees-with-correct`, which needs it, and `false-friend-true-false-marker`. It does not say that a marker's category must agree with `correct`.
data.impact: A producer that reads only the schema may write a `marker` that contradicts `correct`.
data.fix: Add: 'When present, its category must agree with `correct`.'

data.title: Schema `grading` description ignores the exam's grading map
data.snippet:
`inherit`, the default, takes the exam's `grading` value, and
          is `symmetric` outside an exam.
data.description: The exam's `grading` can be a map from question type to strategy (docs/exam.md:333-348); a question then takes the `true-false` entry, or `symmetric` when the key is missing. true-false.md:194-199 says so; the schema description says only 'the exam's `grading` value'.
data.impact: A reader of the schema may think a map value is copied into the question.
data.fix: 'takes the exam's `grading` (its `true-false` entry when it is a map), and is `symmetric` outside an exam or when the exam sets none.'

data.title: `docs/lint-codes.md` makes a `null` feedback or comment a `schema-error`
data.snippet: `null` in these fields is a `schema-error`.
data.description: The `blank-text` row lists the `feedback` and `comment` of a choice, which are OPTIONAL, and ends with '`null` in these fields is a `schema-error`'. question-base.md:103-107 says a `null` in any OPTIONAL field, including nested objects such as choices, is the same as an absent field, and question-base.md:349 repeats it. mdq-py accepts a true/false statement with `feedback: null`.
data.impact: An implementation that follows `docs/lint-codes.md` rejects `feedback: null`, which the base spec and the reference implementation accept.
data.fix: Change the sentence to: '`null` in an OPTIONAL field is an absent field; in a required field it is a `schema-error`.'
data.conditions: A YAML or JSON document with `feedback: null` or `comment: null` on a choice.

data.title: `uniform-true-false-answers` is attached to `choices[].correct`, but reported on `choices`
data.snippet: | choices[].correct  | info     | uniform-true-false-answers               | the statements are all true or all false                   |
data.description: The rule is about the whole list. `examples/valid/true-false/unlisted-marker.lint.json` and mdq-py report it at the path `choices`, and the matching multiple-selection rules (`no-correct-choice`, `all-choices-correct`, multiple-selection.md:161-162) use the field `choices`.
data.impact: An implementation that follows the table reports the info on each statement instead of once on the list, and fails the corpus.
data.fix: Change the Field column to `choices`.

data.title: True/false uses one code where choice questions use `no-correct-choice` and `all-choices-correct`
data.snippet: | choices[].correct  | info     | uniform-true-false-answers               | the statements are all true or all false                   |
data.description: Multiple selection reports a list with no `correct: true` as `no-correct-choice` and a list with every `correct: true` as `all-choices-correct`. True/false has the same field `correct` and the same two cases, but reports both as `uniform-true-false-answers`.
data.impact: A tool that filters diagnostics by code needs a second code for the same property of the same field.
data.fix: Reuse `no-correct-choice` and `all-choices-correct` for true/false, or document why true/false has its own code.

data.title: The introduction calls true statements 'correct answers'
data.snippet:
rendition of a True or False marker. The correct answers are usually marked with
`[T]` and incorrect ones are usually marked with an `[F]`.
data.description: In a true/false question every statement has a correct answer: `[F]` marks a false statement, and the correct answer for it is 'false'. 'Incorrect ones' suggests that `[F]` items are wrong answers, as `[ ]` items are in multiple choice. The Choices section uses the right terms ('true if the statement is true').
data.impact: A reader can confuse the verdict of a statement with the correctness of a student's judgement, which the grading rules depend on.
data.fix: 'True statements are usually marked with `[T]` and false statements with `[F]`.'

data.title: The annex is said to hold a rationale that it does not have
data.snippet:
[annex/true-false-spellings.md](../annex/true-false-spellings.md)
for the source data and the rationale behind each addition.
data.description: `docs/annex/true-false-spellings.md` contains only the spelling table and the references. The rationale for the letter assignments (`S` for TRUE, the letters left in WARNING) is in true-false.md:87-94.
data.impact: A reader who follows the link does not find the rationale.
data.fix: 'for the source data. The rationale follows below.'

data.title: `S` is called the initial of words written in non-Latin scripts
data.snippet:
`S` was chosen for TRUE over FALSE deliberately: it is the initial letter for
"true" in Hindi, Bengali, Arabic, Urdu and Japanese (सत्य, সত্য, صحيح, سچ, 真),
data.description: The cited words are in Devanagari, Bengali, Arabic, Urdu and Han script; `S` is the initial of their romanizations (satya, sahih, sach, shin), from the `ascii` column of the annex. The text does not say so. For Japanese, 真 itself is already a TRUE letter.
data.impact: Minor: the reasoning reads as wrong to a reader who knows these scripts.
data.fix: 'it is the initial of the romanized word for "true" in Hindi, Bengali, Arabic, Urdu and Japanese (satya, satya, sahih, sach, shin)'.

data.title: True/false grading does not define a correct marking, unlike multiple selection
data.snippet:
* **partial**: Each correct marking gives a point, and each incorrect or missing
  marking is ignored.
data.description: multiple-selection.md:107-110 defines 'judged correctly' before the strategies. True/false uses 'correct marking', 'correctly marked', 'incorrect marking' and 'mistake' without saying that a marking is the boolean of the response for a statement and that it is correct when it equals the statement's `correct`. The same property gets different terms in the two documents.
data.impact: A reader must infer how a response value is compared with the answer key.
data.fix: Before the list: 'A statement is **judged correctly** when the response holds its `correct` value, and **judged wrongly** when it holds the other value. An abstention is neither.' Then use these terms in the three strategies.

data.title: No rule for the letter to write when `marker` is absent
data.snippet:
`marker` is OPTIONAL. A document carrying only `correct` is well-formed and
grades identically; it has simply lost the ability to be written back out
unchanged,
data.description: Both implementations serialize questions to MDQ markdown. For a statement with only `correct` (`examples/valid/true-false/no-markers.yaml`), the spec does not say which letter a writer emits: `T`/`F`, or the letters of the `locale` row of the Locale table.
data.impact: Two writers produce different markdown for the same document.
data.fix: State a default: 'A writer that needs a letter for a statement without `marker` SHOULD use the letters of the question's locale from the Locale table, and `T`/`F` otherwise.'

data.title: True/false corpus does not exercise some rules and edge cases
data.snippet: | choices[]          | error    | foreign-choice-marker                    | must use a value allowed in a true/false list              |
data.description: No corpus example covers: `[x]` or `[TRUE]` in a markdown list with `type: true-false` (mdq-py gives `foreign-choice-marker`); a markdown list with a WARNING letter (`unlisted-marker` has only a YAML form); a list whose statements are all false (`uniform-true-false-answers` is tested only for all true); `all-or-nothing` with an abstention on a list whose size gives an inexact score (three statements); a `locale` with an unexpected TRUE letter that is not `T` (`S` under `pt`).
data.impact: Implementations can disagree on these cases without a failing test.
data.fix: Add the examples once the related rules are settled.

data.title: Corpus comment cites multiple-choice.md for the duplicate-text rule
data.snippet:
# are compared with whitespace normalized, so this is `duplicate-choice-text`
# (multiple-choice.md, "Choices"), which JSON Schema cannot express.
data.description: The duplicate-text rule is in `docs/references/choices.md`, section 'Choice text' (lines 115-119). multiple-choice.md 'Choices' only links to it.
data.impact: Minor: the reference is out of date.
data.fix: Cite `references/choices.md, "Choice text"`.

data.text: The true/false schema agrees with the spec on `minItems: 2`, the slug pattern of `id`, the `grading` enum, `shuffle` as boolean or `inherit`, `correct` required and `additionalProperties: false` on statements.
The only complete true/false document in the spec (the Example section) validates with mdq-py with no warning.

data.methodology:
Read docs/references/grammar.md, docs/references/patterns.md, docs/question-types/question-base.md, docs/exam.md, docs/responses.md, docs/references/choices.md and docs/question-types/true-false.md, and checked suspicious rules against the corpus (examples/valid/true-false/, examples/invalid/true-false-*, examples/grading/true-false.yaml) and the reference implementation (mdq-py, `mdq validate`).

A grammar subagent rebuilt the true/false item grammar in Lark, with the TRUE, FALSE and WARNING letter sets built from Unicode General_Category, and tested what it accepts against the prose: letters, case, CJK, symbols, spaces, Unicode spaces, links after the marker, choice ids, feedback and comment blocks, and type inference on mixed lists.

A second subagent scanned true-false.md independently: prose against the Additional Rules table (MUST/SHOULD/MAY against error/warning/info), against schema/true-false.yaml, docs/lint-codes.md and the corpus, and validated the complete example with mdq-py. scripts/spec_audit.py passed before and after the audit.

data.text: The letter test of true/false depends on the Unicode database and the case mapping of each runtime, so Python and JavaScript can disagree on the type and the answer key of the same document.
The same strategy name (`all-or-nothing`) means different things in true/false and in the other types, so an exam-wide `grading` gives inconsistent results.

data.title: [Spec] True/false all-or-nothing must not give partial credit
data.summary: True/false `all-or-nothing` scores `correctly marked / total` when there is no mistake, so abstentions still give partial credit. Options: (a) recommended: 1 only when every statement is judged correctly, an abstention counts as a mistake, as in the glossary, multiple selection and fill-in; (b) keep the rule under a new strategy name and update the glossary and exam.md.
acceptance: true-false.md all-or-nothing agrees with GLOSSARY.md All-or-nothing
The grading table and examples/grading/true-false.yaml agree with the new rule
scripts/spec_audit.py passes

data.title: [Spec] Define the letter test of true/false markers
data.summary: The letter sets exist only in prose, `\p{L}` is outside the regex dialect of grammar.md, the Unicode version is not fixed, the case mapping is not defined (fullwidth `Ｆ` reads as true), `Lm` admits signs such as `ー`, and the NFC info mixes combining sequences with singletons. Recommended: define `TRUE_LETTER`, `FALSE_LETTER` and `WARNING_LETTER` in the snippet; state that the letter test uses General_Category of one code point from a fixed minimum Unicode version; compare after NFKC and case folding (so `Ｆ` is FALSE); restrict WARNING to `Lu`, `Ll`, `Lt`, `Lo`; reword the NFC info for singletons only.
acceptance: The `value` snippet defines `true` and `false`
grammar.md states the exception to the regex dialect for the letter test
The spec fixes the Unicode version and the case mapping
Corpus examples cover fullwidth and long-s markers
scripts/spec_audit.py passes

data.title: [Spec] Define the locale mismatch rule
data.summary: Only one example defines a locale mismatch, the text refers to an absent `id` row, and the prose says MAY for a warning. Recommended: a TRUE or FALSE letter whose folded form is not the expected letter of its category is mismatched; WARNING letters get only `unlisted-true-false-marker`; the prose says SHOULD; delete the `id` row sentence. This is what mdq-py does.
acceptance: true-false.md states which markers are mismatched
The level in prose and table agree
No reference to a missing `id` row
A corpus example covers `S` under `pt`

data.title: [Spec] Settle the rules of the `marker` field
data.summary: The agreement and reserved-`X` rules are only in the table; `malformed-` and `reserved-true-false-marker` overlap with `foreign-choice-marker` in markdown and with `schema-error` in YAML; `marker` is called verbatim but loses the spaces; the schema checks only length; no default letter for writers. Recommended: describe the rules under Choices; say the two marker codes apply to model input and markdown values outside `value` are `foreign-choice-marker`; say a dedicated code replaces `schema-error` for the same field (keep `maxLength`); `marker` is the letter without `ws`; writers use the locale letters, else `T`/`F`.
acceptance: Each marker rule is in prose and table with one code per case
The schema description lists the model rules
scripts/spec_audit.py passes

data.title: [Spec] Reuse the choice-list codes for uniform true/false answers
data.summary: True/false reports both 'all true' and 'all false' as `uniform-true-false-answers`, while multiple selection uses `no-correct-choice` and `all-choices-correct` for the same field. Options: (a) reuse the two codes; (b) recommended: keep the true/false code, since 'all false' is a valid key in true/false and the reason differs, and say so in the prose.
acceptance: true-false.md explains the code or reuses the multiple-selection ones
lint-codes.md agrees

data.title: [Spec] A `null` statement value in a true/false response is an abstention
data.summary: The grading corpus treats `null` as an abstention; docs/responses.md does not. Recommended: say `null` equals an absent key and any other non-boolean is a malformed response.
acceptance: docs/responses.md states the rule for true/false (and multiple selection)

data.title: [Spec] State the error for extra blocks in a choice item
data.summary: A second paragraph, a nested list, a code block or text after the feedback fails the `item` rule, and the spec gives no code. Recommended: `parse-error`, which mdq-py already does.
acceptance: docs/references/choices.md gives the code
An invalid corpus example covers it

data.title: [Spec] Define judged correctly and the value without spaces
data.summary: True/false grading uses 'correct marking' where multiple selection defines 'judged correctly'; type inference says 'a value is a letter' when the value can carry spaces. Recommended: define judged correctly / wrongly / abstention before the strategies, and say inference reads the value without `ws`.
acceptance: true-false.md Grading defines the terms
question-base.md inference trims the value

data.summary: Add the examples listed in the finding once the rules above are settled.
acceptance: Each case in F40 has a corpus example
scripts/spec_audit.py passes

data.text: Make true/false all-or-nothing agree with the glossary and the other types.
Define the letter test formally: letter terminals, Unicode version, case mapping and the NFC info.
Settle the locale and marker rules so each case has one code and one level, in prose and table.
Close the shared gaps: null in responses, extra blocks in choice items, the grading terms and the uniform-answers code.
Apply the mechanical fixes in one pass and extend the corpus.

data.description: The cited words are in Devanagari, Bengali, Arabic, Urdu and Han script; `S` is the initial of their romanizations (satya, sahih, sach, shin), from the `ascii` column of the annex. The text does not say so. For Japanese, U+771F itself is already a TRUE letter.
data.snippet:
`S` was chosen for TRUE over FALSE deliberately: it is the initial letter for
"true" in Hindi, Bengali, Arabic, Urdu and Japanese

data.text: The true-false `value` rule, with `true : /[TtVvSsU+5BF9U+771F]/`, `false : /[FfU+9519U+507D]/` and the WARNING class built from General_Category, accepts `[T]`, `[t]`, `[V]`, `[S]`, `[F]`, `[f]`, `[U+5BF9]`, `[U+771F]`, `[U+9519]`, `[U+507D]`, `[ T ]`, `[\tT\t]`, `[é]` (U+00E9) and the astral letter U+20000, and rejects `[X]`, `[x]`, `[TF]`, `[ ]`, `[]`, `[✓]`, `[×]`, `[U+3007]`, `[1]`, `[*]` and `[e\u0301]`, as the prose states (Lark Earley test).

No compatibility ideograph whose NFC form is a TRUE or FALSE letter changes the meaning: the only ones found, U+2F946 and U+2F947 (NFC U+771F), are WARNING letters and so also mean true (scan of all `\p{L}` code points with `unicodedata`, Unicode 15.1).

data.summary: The letter sets exist only in prose, `\p{L}` is outside the regex dialect of grammar.md, the Unicode version is not fixed, the case mapping is not defined (fullwidth `U+FF26` reads as true), `Lm` admits signs such as `U+30FC`, and the NFC info mixes combining sequences with singletons. Recommended: define `TRUE_LETTER`, `FALSE_LETTER` and `WARNING_LETTER` in the snippet; state that the letter test uses General_Category of one code point from a fixed minimum Unicode version; compare after NFKC and case folding (so `U+FF26` is FALSE); restrict WARNING to `Lu`, `Ll`, `Lt`, `Lo`; reword the NFC info for singletons only.

data.description: `Lm` and `Lo` contain characters that read as punctuation or symbols: `ˆ` (U+02C6), `U+30FC` (U+30FC KATAKANA-HIRAGANA PROLONGED SOUND MARK, looks like a dash), `U+3005` (U+3005), and the ordinal indicators `ª` (U+00AA) and `º` (U+00BA), common in pt-BR. Counter-example: `* [U+30FC] a` is accepted as a WARNING letter and means true, while the spec excludes `✓`, `×` and `U+3007` because they are not letters.

`U+0915U+093C` U+0958 DEVANAGARI LETTER QA is one `Lo` code point, so `* [U+0915U+093C] a` is a valid WARNING marker (accepted in the test). Its NFC form is two code points (U+0915 U+093C, a composition exclusion). An editor or pipeline that normalizes to NFC turns the valid marker into a `foreign-choice-marker`. Conversely, `[é]` is valid as U+00E9 and invalid as `e` + U+0301. The spec does not say whether the parser normalizes the source.

data.fix: `T`, `V`, `S`, `U+5BF9` and `U+771F`; the same for the FALSE line.
data.snippet: * **TRUE**: `TVS`, plus

data.description: No snippet defines `true` or `false`; `scripts/spec_audit.py` compiles the snippet only with stubs. The letter sets exist only in prose (lines 83-98), and the WARNING category, which means true, is not visible in the rule. A reader cannot tell from the grammar that `[Q]` matches `true`. Testing needed a hand-built grammar: `true : /[TtVvSsU+5BF9U+771F]/`, `false : /[FfU+9519U+507D]/`, and a third alternative for every other letter except `X`/`x`.

grammar.md ("Regex dialect") says terminals use only explicit character classes that match the same characters in Python `re`, JavaScript `RegExp` and JSON Schema `pattern`. `\p{L}` does not meet this: `re.compile(r'\p{L}')` raises `bad escape \p` in Python 3.13; in JavaScript without the `u` flag, `/^\p{L}$/` is a literal `p{L}` and does not match `p` or `U+771F`; without `u`, `/^[^\]]$/` does not match U+20000 (two UTF-16 units). Lark's default `re` backend cannot use it either; the explicit class built from `unicodedata` for the test is about 10 KB.

'Incompatible with the locale' is defined only by one example (`T` under `pt`). Open cases: is `S`, `U+5BF9` or `U+9519` under `pt` mismatched? Is a WARNING letter such as `W` under `pt` also mismatched, or only `unlisted-true-false-marker`? Is lowercase `t` mismatched (case-insensitive)? mdq-py warns for every TRUE or FALSE letter outside the expected pair, case-insensitively, and never for a WARNING letter: under `pt-BR` it flags `S`, `t`, `U+5BF9`, `U+9519` and not `W`.

The spec does not say which case mapping applies. mdq-py uses case folding: `[ſ]` (U+017F LATIN SMALL LETTER LONG S) folds to `s` and reads as TRUE with no warning. The fullwidth letters that CJK input methods produce are WARNING letters: `[U+FF26]` (U+FF26) reads as true with only `unlisted-true-false-marker`, so a statement the author marked false is graded as true. A titlecase letter (`Lt`, such as U+01C5) is a WARNING letter too.
data.fix: Define the comparison: for example, NFKC then case folding before the category lookup, so `U+FF26` is FALSE and `ſ` is TRUE. Or keep exact comparison of the letter and its simple lowercase, and make a fullwidth `U+FF34`/`U+FF26` an error. Add corpus examples for the chosen rule.
data.impact: Implementations that use lowercase mapping, case folding or NFKC give different categories for the same marker. The fullwidth `U+FF26` case flips the answer key with only a warning.

data.description: Cyrillic `U+0422` (U+0422), `U+0425` (U+0425) and Greek `U+03A4` (U+03A4), `U+03A7` (U+03A7) look like `T` and `X`. A list of only Cyrillic `[U+0425]` items is inferred as true/false and every statement reads as true, with `unlisted-true-false-marker`. Russian 'U+0432U+0435U+0440U+043DU+043E' starts with Cyrillic `U+0412`, which looks like Latin `B`. The warning catches these, but its message cannot tell the author why.
